title: The City of God (after 410)
hookLine: Rome is sacked, and Augustine writes of two cities built by two loves
tomorrow: Love, and do what you will

cards: News crosses the sea to North Africa: Rome has been sacked by the Goths. Not a border town. Rome.
The city that had seemed as permanent as the sky. Refugees arrive with stories.

And some who still honor the old gods say out loud what others are whispering: this is what happens when an empire abandons its gods for the Christian one. Augustine, a bishop in a harbor town, hears it.
He doesn't answer with a quick sermon. He starts writing, book after book, until the answer becomes the work he calls The City of God.

teach.b: First, the question underneath. If God is on our side, how could Rome fall? Augustine moves the ground.
No city on earth was ever God's guarantee. Empires rise and fall; something else is being built. Second, the heart of it, in book fourteen.
Two loves, he says, have made two cities. The earthly city is built by love of self, reaching even to contempt of God. The heavenly city is built by love of God, reaching even to contempt of self.
The line runs by love, not by address. Rome is not simply the earthly city.
And though Augustine can call the Church the city of God, he says that on earth even the Church holds some who will not share its end, while some of its present enemies will.
Third, in this world the two cities are mixed together, tangled, until the last judgment. Some readers hear Jesus's parable of the wheat and the weeds in that. You can't draw a map.
The same street, the same family, sometimes the same heart, holds both loves pulling against each other. Fourth, how to live in the meantime.

teach.h: A PILGRIM CITY ON THE ROAD.
teach.b: Augustine calls the city of God a pilgrim on earth.
Pilgrims don't despise the towns they pass through. They use the roads, keep the peace, pray for the place, the way the prophet Jeremiah told the exiles in Babylon to seek the peace of the city.
But they don't mistake it for home. For Augustine, Rome's fall was terrible and real, but not the end of the story. For him, the city that mattered most had never had walls.

how: When the Second Vatican Council describes the Church in Lumen Gentium 8, it quotes The City of God on the Church pressing forward like a pilgrim, amid the world's persecutions and God's consolations.

games.q: Rome has been sacked, and your neighbors blame the Christians. you're Augustine. where do you draw the line between the two cities?
o: between two loves, running through every heart.
games.why: two loves made two cities, he says: love of self and love of God. they're mixed together until the end, so you can't draw them on a map.

practice: Look back over the last day at three things you did with real effort: a task, a conversation, a decision. For each, ask gently: which love was doing the building, love of self, or love turned toward God or someone else's good?
A day can hold both; if you pray, offer tomorrow's work to God.

wordCard.voice: civitas Dei. Latin for the city of God, Augustine's name for the heavenly city built by love of God, tangled with the earthly one until the end. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: two loves, two cities. The question is always which love is building. That's day seven hundred thirty-nine.
